fatal_errors: The proposed Ti/TiC microalloying intervention does not reconstruct the target intervention: liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h.
The initial material is misidentified as an already formed W–Cu composite rather than the single-BCC WTaVTi dendrite–interdendrite precursor.

The proposed TiC interphase and void-suppression mechanism replace the target selective Ti–Cu exchange, retention of W/Ta/V-rich ligaments, and spontaneous approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer.
The cited evidence concerns Ti/Ni-coated diamond in an HEA matrix and does not establish TiC formation, interfacial compatibility, or improved thermal conductivity in W–Cu.
No evidence supports the claim that residual carbon plus 0.5–2 wt% Ti will create a uniform nanoscale TiC layer rather than discrete carbides or a thermally resistive reaction layer.
The irradiation claim improperly extends generic interfacial stability to relevant irradiation service without specifying particle, energy, fluence, temperature, or damage mechanism.
explanation: The hypothesis shares only the broad application goal of improving thermal transport and interface integrity in W/Cu-related joints. It misses the target precursor, liquid-metal-dealloying intervention, bicontinuous aligned RHEA–Cu architecture, W-rich interlayer, and the measured temperature-dependent and He-implantation outcomes. The similar 1200 °C temperature is incidental because the proposed atmosphere, reaction route, and duration differ. The comparative experiment could test the proposed TiC concept at a basic level, but it lacks a Ti-only versus Ti-plus-carbon factorial control and a specified irradiation protocol, so it would not decisively attribute any benefit to TiC. Most importantly, the supplied diamond/HEA evidence is not transferable enough to support improved W–Cu thermal conductivity or irradiation resistance.
